title: Microsoft Unveils MDASH, an AI Security System That Outperforms Anthropic's Mythos in Vulnerability Detection
excerpt: The multi-model agentic system orchestrates over 100 specialized AI agents to find and verify real-world software bugs, scoring 88.45% on the CyberGym benchmark.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft's MDASH scored 88.45% on CyberGym, outperforming Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5.
  • MDASH utilizes over 100 specialized AI agents for comprehensive software vulnerability detection.
  • The system achieved 96% recall on five years of Microsoft Security Response Center cases.
  • Microsoft is integrating Anthropic's Mythos into its security framework through Project Glasswing.
  • The AI security arms race is reshaping job functions for engineers in major tech firms.

  • Microsoft's MDASH (Multi-model Agentic Scanning Harness) scored 88.45% on the CyberGym benchmark, surpassing Anthropic's Mythos at 83.1% and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 at 81.8%.
  • The system orchestrates over 100 specialized AI agents across multiple models to discover, debate, and prove software vulnerabilities end-to-end.
  • MDASH identified 16 Windows vulnerabilities fixed in the latest Patch Tuesday update, achieving 96% recall against five years of confirmed MSRC cases.
  • Microsoft also integrated Anthropic's Mythos into its Security Development Lifecycle through the Project Glasswing partnership.

The race to weaponize artificial intelligence for cybersecurity defense took a sharp turn this week as Microsoft revealed MDASH, an internally developed multi-model system that has surpassed Anthropic's high-profile Mythos model on key vulnerability detection benchmarks.

What MDASH Does Differently

While Anthropic's Mythos operates as a single powerful AI model within an agent framework, MDASH takes a fundamentally different approach. It orchestrates more than 100 specialized AI agents across an ensemble of frontier and distilled models, each assigned to a specific role in the vulnerability discovery pipeline.

Some agents scan code for potential flaws. Another group debates whether each discovery is real and exploitable. A final set constructs proof-of-concept attacks to confirm the bugs are genuine. The result is what Microsoft vice president Taesoo Kim described as a system that can "discover, debate, and prove exploitable bugs end-to-end."

"The results speak for themselves: 21 of 21 planted vulnerabilities found with zero false positives on a private test driver."

— Taesoo Kim, Microsoft Vice President

Benchmark Performance

On the CyberGym benchmark — a UC Berkeley-created test using 1,507 real-world vulnerability tasks across 188 open-source projects — MDASH scored 88.45%, roughly five points ahead of Anthropic's Mythos at 83.1% and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 at 81.8%.

In testing against Microsoft's own codebases, the system achieved 96% recall against five years of confirmed Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) cases in Windows' clfs.sys driver and 100% in the TCP/IP stack. MDASH identified 16 of the vulnerabilities that Microsoft patched in its latest Patch Tuesday update.

Microsoft's Dual Strategy

The MDASH announcement came alongside Microsoft's deepening partnership with Anthropic. Through Project Glasswing — a controlled initiative involving more than 45 organizations including Apple, Google, and Amazon — Microsoft has been evaluating Mythos for its Security Development Lifecycle since April.

Ales Holecek, Microsoft's chief architect for security, said the company evaluated Mythos using its CTI-REALM benchmark and found "substantial improvements relative to prior models." Microsoft plans to embed both Mythos and MDASH into its secure coding framework, effectively running competitor and homegrown systems in parallel.

A Three-Way Race in AI Security

The field is moving rapidly. Anthropic's Mythos has already found "thousands" of major vulnerabilities in operating systems and browsers. Mozilla reported significant success using it to fix Firefox vulnerabilities. The NSA has been testing Mythos to probe Microsoft products, according to Bloomberg.

OpenAI entered the competition with Daybreak, its own agentic security offering integrated with the Codex coding tool. CEO Sam Altman wrote that "AI is already good and about to get super good at cybersecurity."

Why It Matters for the Tech Workforce

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin engineers working across Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and cybersecurity firms, the AI security arms race is reshaping job functions in real time. Security engineers who previously spent weeks manually auditing code are increasingly orchestrating AI agents to do the heavy lifting — a transition that demands new skills but also amplifies individual productivity.

Microsoft patched a record 570 security flaws in its latest update cycle, a 4x increase from the same period last year. The company attributed the surge in part to AI-accelerated attacks — a trend that makes AI-powered defense not just useful but necessary.
